content: The methodologies were consistently implemented across all study participants in the referenced studies (32-39, 42-48, 58, 59). For these studies, the risk of bias in this domain was considered low. However, one study (48) provided limited details on the outcome measure, making it difficult to assess its validity. Due to this lack of detail, the study was rated as having a high risk of bias in this domain. Regarding the blinding of outcome assessors, none of the 17 studies provided methodological details about potential blinding or masking of outcome assessors. Consequently, it must be assumed that no blinding was performed. This lack of blinding could pose a significant concern for those conducting data analysis, as knowledge of the exposure status of study participants could introduce bias when examining relationships with outcomes. Therefore, these studies were rated as having a medium to high risk of bias in this domain. For follow-up rates, bias due to loss to follow-up was not applicable in 13 of the included studies (35-39, 42-48, 58) because they were observational by design. However, four studies had a loss to follow-up rate of 20% or less (32-34, 59), and these were rated as having a low risk of bias. In terms of statistical analyses, 12 of the included studies accounted for confounding variables (33-39, 42, 43, 45, 47, 58), and these were rated as having a low risk of bias in this category. However, for two studies (32, 59), it was not possible to determine the confounding variables, leading to a medium risk of bias rating. Regarding study design, 12 studies reported the frequency of animal-source food (ASF) consumption among children. All of these studies were observational (32-34, 36-39, 42-46). Among them, seven studies used a cross-sectional design (32-34, 36, 37, 42, 45), three used prospective cohort designs (38, 43, 44), and two used longitudinal designs (39, 46). The study populations included children aged 0-12 years, with specific age ranges varying by study: 6-23 months (32, 34), 0-12 months (33), 1 year (36), 6-42 months (37), 1-12 years (39), 6-12 months (42), 0-48 months (38), 12 months to 5 years (43), 12-24 months (44), 6-36 months (45), and 12-23 months (46). The studies were conducted in various geographical locations. Five studies were conducted in Asia, including two in Indonesia (32, 46), two in Japan (36, 43), and one in Myanmar (45). Three studies were conducted in Africa, with one each in Senegal (37), Somalia (34), and South Africa (33). Three studies were conducted in Europe, with one each in Israel (44), the Netherlands (38), and Sweden (39). One study was conducted in South America, specifically in Brazil (42). The reported outcomes included stunting (32, 45), wasting (32, 45), underweight (32, 45), and anemia (42, 44). For stunting, Ahmad et al. (2018) assessed children aged 6-23 months who consumed meat. No significant differences in stunting were observed among children consuming meat ≥3 times per week, 1-2 times per week, or never (GRADE = very low). Similarly, Zhao et al. (2016) found no differences in stunting among children aged 6-36 months who consumed meat at varying frequencies (GRADE = very low). For wasting, Ahmad et al. (2018) reported no differences in wasting among children consuming meat ≥3 times per week, 1-2 times per week, or never (GRADE = very low). Zhao et al. (2016) also found no differences in wasting among children aged 6-36 months who consumed meat at varying frequencies (GRADE = very low). For underweight, Ahmad et al. (2018) observed a significantly higher risk of underweight in children consuming meat 1-2 times per week compared to those who never consumed meat (GRADE = very low). However, no differences were observed between children consuming meat ≥3 times per week and those consuming meat 1-2 times per week. For anemia, Silva et al. (2007) assessed children aged 6-12 months who consumed red meat. A potential reduction in anemia was observed in children consuming red meat daily or weekly compared to those consuming it less than weekly. Additionally, a significantly lower risk of anemia was reported in children who consumed red meat in the past 24 hours compared to those who did not (GRADE = very low). For egg consumption, Ahmad et al. (2018) and Zhao et al. (2016) assessed stunting, wasting, and underweight in children aged 6-36 months. No significant differences were observed in any of these outcomes based on the frequency of egg consumption (GRADE = very low). For fish consumption, Ahmad et al. (2018) assessed stunting, wasting, and underweight in children aged 6-23 months. No significant differences in stunting or underweight were observed based on fish consumption frequency. However, a significant 48% reduction in wasting was reported among children consuming fish ≥4 times per week compared to those consuming fish 1-3 times per week (GRADE = very low).
